name: ESP32-C3FH4
title: ESP32-C3 series: RISC-V Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE SoC in QFN32 5×5 mm, with optional 4 or 8 MB flash in the package
summary: A single-chip 2.4 GHz radio microcontroller: one 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IMC) at up to 160 MHz with 384 KB ROM, 400 KB SRAM and 8 KB RTC SRAM, 802.11b/g/n Wi-Fi to 150 Mbps and Bluetooth 5 LE with coded PHY, sharing one RF port with its balun, switch, PA and LNA on chip. It runs from 3.0 to 3.6 V, needs an external main crystal, and sleeps at 5 µA in Deep-sleep. The variants differ in flash: ESP32-C3 has none and uses external SPI flash; ESP32-C3FN4, -FH4, -FH4AZ and -FH4X carry 4 MB and -FH8X 8 MB inside the package. The -FH4AZ and -FH4X leave the flash pins unbonded and offer 16 GPIOs, the rest 22. ESP32-C3FH4 is rated for -40 to 105 °C ambient.
key_figures: 32-bit RISC-V single core, up to 160 MHz; 483.27 CoreMark (3.02 CoreMark/MHz)
384 KB ROM, 400 KB SRAM (16 KB for cache), 8 KB RTC SRAM, 4096-bit eFuse (1792 bits for users)
22, of which 3 strapping and 6 used by the flash
3.0 ~ 3.6 V, supply able to give 0.5 A
Bluetooth 5, 2402 ~ 2480 MHz; up to 20 dBm TX; -105 dBm typ RX (125 Kbps)
5 µA typ (RTC timer and RTC memory on)
QFN32 5×5 mm, 0.5 mm pitch, exposed pad

notes: Name fields, left to right: ESP32-C3 (series); F (flash inside the package); H or N (flash temperature grade, high or normal); flash size in MB; AZ (another identification code); X (chip revision v1.1).
Ambient temperature is the recommended range for the air immediately round the chip.
The in-package flash runs at up to 80 MHz and has no auto-suspend by default; a 120 MHz flash clock or auto-suspend is available on request.
Every revision has the same SRAM, but v1.1 leaves about 10 KB more free for the user than v0.4, and v1.1 needs particular ESP-IDF versions.
ESP32-C3 has no flash inside and needs an external SPI flash.
The 16-GPIO variants leave the SPI0/SPI1 flash pins unbonded.

tables.title: Pin overview
notes: Default function set in the default boot mode: IO MUX for pins 4 to 6, 8 to 10, 12 to 16 and 19 to 24, 27 and 28; Analog (USB) for GPIO18 and GPIO19. VDD_SPI defaults to its power role.
IE: input enabled. WPU: weak pull-up on. WPD: weak pull-down on. USB_PU: USB pull-up on.
A pin listed as powered by VDD_SPI really draws from the internal rail that feeds VDD_SPI. Whether pins 19 to 24 run from VDD3P3_CPU or VDD_SPI is set by a register.
Default drive strength: 10 mA on GPIO2, GPIO3, MTMS and MTDI; 40 mA on GPIO18 and GPIO19; 20 mA on every other pin.

GPIO18 and GPIO19 start in USB mode, where the pull-up comes from the USB pull-up resistor (USB_SERIAL_JTAG_DP/DM_PULLUP, value set by USB_SERIAL_JTAG_PULLUP_VALUE). With USB turned off they are plain GPIOs whose weak pulls start off (IO_MUX_FUN_WPU/WPD).
6: with EFUSE_DIS_PAD_JTAG = 0 (unburnt default) MTCK has IE and WPU after reset; with it burnt, IE only.
7: U0TXD has its output enabled after reset.
8: VDD_SPI feeds the in-package and any external flash by default. It can become a GPIO when an external flash has its own supply.
9: pins 19 to 24 are not bonded on ESP32-C3FH4AZ and ESP32-C3FH4X and are marked NC.

operation.text: One 32-bit RISC-V core, RV32IMC, with a four-stage pipeline at up to 160 MHz, a 32-bit multiplier and divider, up to 32 vectored interrupts on seven priority levels, up to 8 hardware breakpoints or watchpoints, up to 16 PMP regions, and JTAG debug. The interrupt matrix maps 62 peripheral interrupt sources onto 31 CPU interrupts, each with settable priority, type, threshold and enable.

The general DMA controller has three transmit and three receive channels, shared among SPI2, UHCI0, I2S, AES, SHA and the ADC. Channels work from linked lists, carry peripheral-to-memory and memory-to-memory traffic, all reach internal RAM, and are arbitrated by a fixed but configurable priority.

384 KB of ROM holds boot and core routines. 400 KB of SRAM serves code and data at up to 160 MHz, 16 KB of it set aside as cache. 8 KB of RTC FAST SRAM is reachable by the CPU and keeps its contents in Deep-sleep. 4 Kbit of eFuse holds system settings, of which 1792 bits are for user data such as keys and a device ID; eFuse bits are one-time programmable, 0 unburnt and 1 burnt, with configurable read and write protection and error-coding.

SPI, dual SPI, quad SPI and QPI flash outside the package can be attached, up to 16 MB, and the CPU can map instructions and read-only data from it: up to 8 MB of instruction space and 8 MB of data space at a time, each in 64 KB blocks, with 8-, 16- and 32-bit reads. The read-only cache is 16 KB, eight-way set-associative, with 32-byte blocks, pre-load, lock, and critical-word-first with early restart. Software can change the flash mapping once the chip is running. Flash contents can be protected by XTS-AES encryption.

On ESP32-C3FN4, -FH4 and -FH8X the flash inside the package hangs on SPICLK, SPICS0, SPID, SPIQ, SPIWP and SPIHD (pins 19 to 24) and those pins are not to be used for anything else. On -FH4X and -FH4AZ the same flash is wired inside and pins 19 to 24 are not bonded. ESP32-C3 has no internal flash; the same six pins are the advised connection for an external one. VDD_SPI powers the flash by default.

There are 22 GPIOs (16 on -FH4X and -FH4AZ). Each IO pin can take one of three IO MUX functions, F0 to F2: a fixed direct link to UART0, JTAG, SPI0/1 or SPI2, or a route through the GPIO matrix, which lets almost any peripheral input come from any pin and any output go to any pin at the cost of some added delay. Every GPIO has selectable pull-up, pull-down or high impedance, can raise edge- or level-triggered interrupts, is a non-inverting tri-state buffer, and can be held in its state for low-power operation. Some pins also carry ADC, USB or 32 kHz crystal functions.

GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are strapping pins. GPIO18 and GPIO19 start as the USB Serial/JTAG D- and D+ and must be reconfigured to act as GPIOs. GPIO4 to GPIO7 carry JTAG, which can be freed by debugging over the USB pins instead. GPIO20 and GPIO21 carry UART0, often used for debug. GPIO11 is VDD_SPI and becomes a GPIO only when the flash has its own supply. GPIO12 to GPIO17 belong to the flash.

GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are latched at chip reset (power-up or CHIP_EN) and the latched values stay until power-down; nothing else changes them, and the pins then work as ordinary IOs. GPIO9 has a weak pull-up at reset and GPIO2 and GPIO8 float, so set levels with external pull resistors or from a host MCU. The levels must be in place no later than CHIP_EN rising (tSU 0 ms) and held for 3 ms after (tH). Two eFuses also bear on boot, EFUSE_UART_PRINT_CONTROL for UART0 messages and EFUSE_USB_PRINT_CHANNEL for USB messages; both default to 0.

GPIO9 high gives SPI boot, where the ROM loader runs the program in SPI flash. GPIO9 low with GPIO8 high gives joint download boot, where a binary can be written to flash over UART0 or USB, or loaded into SRAM and run from there. GPIO2 does not take part in the choice but should be pulled up because of glitches. A further SPI download boot mode exists (Technical Reference Manual).

During early SPI boot the ROM prints to UART0 and to the USB Serial/JTAG controller by default. UART0 output is governed by EFUSE_UART_PRINT_CONTROL together with GPIO8, USB output by EFUSE_USB_PRINT_CHANNEL and EFUSE_DIS_USB_SERIAL_JTAG; either can be silenced.

VDD3P3_RTC feeds the RTC IO pins and the low-power 1.1 V regulator for the RTC domain. The digital system 1.1 V regulator draws on both VDD3P3_RTC and VDD3P3_CPU. VDD3P3_CPU feeds the digital IO pins and, through RSPI (7.5 Ω typ), the VDD_SPI pin that supplies the flash and the SPI IO pins. VDDA (two pins) and VDD3P3 (two pins) supply the analog and RF circuits. All supply pins are 3.0 to 3.6 V, from a source able to deliver 0.5 A in total; keep VDD3P3_CPU at or below 3.3 V while burning eFuses.

CHIP_EN is raised only after the VDDA, VDD3P3, VDD3P3_RTC and VDD3P3_CPU rails have passed 2.8 V and settled for tSTBL, at least 50 µs. Pulling CHIP_EN below VIL_nRST (0.25 × VDD) for at least 50 µs (tRST) resets the chip; it is released above VIH_nRST (0.75 × VDD). CHIP_EN low powers the chip off (1 µA typ). CHIP_EN must not float. At power-up MTCK, MTDO, GPIO10 and U0RXD drive low for about 5 ns and GPIO18 drives high for about 50 µs.

Four reset levels: CPU reset restarts the core only; core reset clears the whole digital system apart from RTC (CPU, peripherals, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE, digital GPIOs); system reset also clears RTC; chip reset clears everything. All but chip reset keep internal memory contents. Resets come from software, by register, or from hardware.

The CPU clock comes from the external main crystal, the fast RC oscillator (about 17.5 MHz, trimmable) or the PLL, directly or divided; after reset it runs on the crystal divided by 2. The chip will not run without the main crystal. The RTC slow clock (for the RTC counter and watchdog and the low-power controller) comes from an external 32 kHz crystal, the internal slow RC oscillator (about 136 kHz, trimmable) or the fast RC divided by 256. The RTC fast clock comes from the crystal divided by 2 or the fast RC divided by N (about 17.5 MHz).

Active: CPU, radio and peripherals all on. Modem-sleep: the CPU runs, possibly at a lower clock, and the radio switches on only when the wireless link needs it; Wi-Fi is clock-gated (13 to 28 mA). Light-sleep: the CPU stops and may stay powered, some digital peripheral groups can be shut off, links can stay up, and wake-up comes from the MAC, the RTC timer or an external interrupt (130 µA typ). Deep-sleep: only the RTC domain stays powered and wireless link state is kept in RTC memory (5 µA typ).

A 52-bit system timer has two counters at a fixed 16 MHz and three comparators, with target or period alarms (52-bit target, 26-bit period), auto-reload, three interrupts, and stalling with the CPU or in OCD mode. Two 54-bit general-purpose timers have 16-bit prescalers (1 to 65536), count up or down, can be read live, halted and resumed, and raise level interrupts on alarm. Three digital watchdogs (one in each timer group, one in RTC) have four stages each with their own timeout, a 32-bit counter and write protection; the RTC watchdog and the timer-group-0 watchdog start by themselves during flash boot and restart the system if boot stalls. An analog super watchdog runs at ultra-low power with an early-warning interrupt. The XTAL32K watchdog switches the RTC slow clock to another source if the 32 kHz crystal stops.

Secure boot and XTS-AES flash encryption (IEEE 1619-2007, automatic decryption) protect code. Hardware accelerators: AES-128/256 with ECB, CBC, OFB, CTR, CFB8 and CFB128 in DMA mode; SHA-1, SHA-224 and SHA-256; RSA up to 3072-bit modular exponentiation and multiplication and 1536-bit multiplication; HMAC-SHA-256 that can feed keys to the RSA digital signature peripheral or re-enable soft-disabled JTAG; RSA digital signatures to 3072 bits with an encrypted private key. A true random number generator draws on ADC thermal noise and clock mismatch. A permission controller splits memory and peripherals between privileged and unprivileged environments, and the World Controller separates a secure and a non-secure world. Glitches on the crystal clock trigger a reset of the whole digital circuit including RTC. A debug assistant watches bus reads and writes, the stack pointer, the last PC before reset and selected bus writes.

Two UARTs to 5 Mbps (RS232, RS485, IrDA) with hardware and software flow control, reachable by DMA through UHCI0. SPI0 and SPI1 serve the flash (single, dual, quad SPI and QPI, up to 120 MHz STR); SPI2 is a general master or slave with DMA: as master 80 MHz in full-duplex or 1-, 2-, 4-line half-duplex with six chip selects and settable CS timing, as slave 60 MHz. One I2C controller, master or slave, at 100 kbit/s, 400 kbit/s and up to 800 kbit/s depending on pull-up strength, 7- and 10-bit addressing. One I2S, master or slave, 8 to 32-bit words, BCK 10 kHz to 40 MHz, TDM and PDM. A USB 2.0 full-speed (12 Mbit/s) Serial/JTAG controller with its own PHY gives a CDC-ACM port and a JTAG adapter for flashing and debugging. A TWAI (CAN 2.0, ISO 11898-1) controller runs from 1 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s with standard and extended frames, a 64-byte receive FIFO and acceptance filters. The LED PWM controller has six channels with duty resolution to 14 bits, hardware fades, and runs in Light-sleep. The remote control peripheral has two transmit and two receive channels sharing 192 × 32 bits of memory.

Two 12-bit SAR ADCs: ADC1 measures 5 channels (GPIO0 to GPIO4) and is calibrated in the factory; ADC2 measures one channel (GPIO5) and is not. ADC2 does not work on some chip revisions (see the SoC errata). Four attenuation settings give ranges of 0 to 750, 1050, 1300 and 2500 mV.
An internal sensor covers -40 °C to 125 °C through an ADC. It tracks the die, which usually runs warmer than the surrounding air, and its reading moves with clock speed and I/O load.

On chip the radio has a 2.4 GHz receiver and transmitter, its own bias circuits and regulators, a balun with a TX/RX switch, and a clock generator whose inductors, varactors, filters and dividers are all internal. The receiver has RF filters, automatic gain control, DC offset cancellation and baseband filters, and converts to digital with two fast ADCs. The CMOS power amplifier is linearised by digital calibration, and further calibrations correct carrier leakage, I/Q mismatch, baseband and RF nonlinearity and antenna matching.

802.11b/g/n, 1T1R, 20 and 40 MHz channels, MCS0 to 7 and MCS32, 0.4 µs guard interval, RX STBC, up to 150 Mbps, adjustable TX power, and antenna diversity through an external RF switch driven from GPIOs. The MAC runs station, SoftAP, station plus SoftAP and promiscuous modes over four virtual interfaces, with A-MPDU, A-MSDU, immediate block ACK, TXOP, WMM, RTS/CTS, hardware beacon monitoring, 802.11mc FTM and WEP, TKIP, CCMP, GCMP, WAPI, BIP, WPA2 and WPA3 security. While scanning as a station the SoftAP channel follows the station channel. Software libraries cover TCP/IP, ESP-WIFI-MESH and TLS 1.0 to 1.2.

Bluetooth 5 LE and Bluetooth mesh, with 1 Mbps, 2 Mbps and coded 125 and 500 Kbps PHYs, hardware listen-before-talk, and a high-power mode up to 20 dBm. The link layer supports advertising extensions, several advertising sets, advertising while scanning, several connections in central and peripheral roles together, adaptive frequency hopping, channel selection algorithm #2, LE privacy 1.2, data length extension, link-layer encryption and LE ping. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share one antenna through an internal coexistence scheme.

RF figures are taken at the antenna port through a cable, front-end loss included, with a 0 Ω resistor as the front-end circuit, from 3.3 V (±5 %) at 25 °C. Centre frequency and target power are set in software; use only the channels the local regulator allows.
ESP32-C3, -FN4, -FH4 and -FH4AZ are revision v0.4; -FH4X and -FH8X are v1.1. The errata document lists what each revision fixes and which ESP-IDF releases support it.

QFN32, 5 × 5 mm body, 0.85 mm nominal height, 32 pads at 0.5 mm pitch with a 3.7 mm square exposed ground pad (pin 33) and a C0.300 chamfer marking pin 1 on the pad; a dot marks pin 1 on top. Dimensions and tolerances follow JEDEC MO-220. A land-pattern file is offered as DXF.
